Watch · Step 4 of 5A Proxy for the SiteThe reverse proxy opens the sealNow there’s no proxy on your side, but techconcepts.app has a reverse proxy in front of its server. The site’s address, 198.51.100.7, now leads to the reverse proxy, and the web server sits behind it. The reverse proxy holds the site’s certificate, so your sealed line ends there. It opens the seal and reads your request.Go deeperthe technical detailsEnding HTTPS at the reverse proxy saves the servers behind it that work, and lets the reverse proxy read each request to choose where it goes.71112techconcepts.app’s address198.51.100.7, now the reverse proxy’sYour sealed lineends at the reverse proxyThe web serverbehind it, at 10.0.0.20

Watch · Step 5 of 5Passed to the ServerYour address goes along in a headerThe reverse proxy passes your request to the web server on a connection of its own, as plain HTTP. So the server sees the reverse proxy’s address, 10.0.0.2. Your address goes along in a header, X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.23. The page comes back the same way, and the reverse proxy seals it for you.Go deeperthe technical detailsA reverse proxy can keep a copy of the page and give it to the next reader without asking the server, but only if the site’s response allows it. A response marked no-store or private isn’t kept for others.1314The server sees10.0.0.2, the reverse proxyYour addressin X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.23Inside the siteplain HTTP, to port 80A reverse proxy can alsospread requests over servers, or answer from a copy

networking/load-balancers: OverviewOne server can only take so many readers at once, and any server can fail. So example.net puts a load balancer in front of three servers. Readers use one address, the balancer passes each request to a server, and it checks every server again and again. Watch one fail its checks, get skipped, and come back.Load BalancerLoad balancerThink of a supermarket with one person at the front pointing each shopper to a till. A till whose light is off is skipped until it comes back on.This lesson: Watch›Learn›PracticeQuick factsDoespasses each new request to a server in its poolReaders useone address, the balancer’sChecksevery server, again and againA failing servergets no new requests until it passes againOSI layer4 or 7, depending on the balancer

Watch · Step 1 of 5One Address, Three ServersYou reach the balancer, not a serverYou ask example.net for its page. Its address, 203.0.113.80, belongs to a load balancer, not to a server. Behind it are three servers, A, B and C: its pool. They have private addresses, so readers only ever use the balancer’s. Watch · Step 2 of 5Spread Across the PoolEach new request to the next serverTwo more readers ask for the page. This balancer takes the servers in turn, called round robin: the next request goes to B, the one after to C. That’s one way to spread the load. Other balancers favour the servers with fewer requests in progress, or pick by a hash of each connection. Either way, no one server gets every reader.Go deeperthe technical detailsWith a hash, the balancer mixes a connection’s five values (both addresses, both ports and the protocol) into a number that picks the server. B misses the next one too, so the balancer marks it unhealthy.Go deeperthe technical detailsHow often to check, and how many missed checks in a row count, are settings chosen by whoever runs the balancer. networking/vpn: OverviewOn a café’s Wi-Fi you can’t tell who is listening. A VPN wraps what you send through it in a sealed packet addressed to a VPN server, so all the café sees of it is that you’re talking to the server. But the seal ends at the server: from there your request goes on as it would have without the VPN. Watch both, and see why HTTPS still matters.VPNVirtual private networkThink of putting your postcard in a sealed envelope addressed to a friend, who opens it and posts the postcard on. Until your friend, everyone sees only the envelope; after, it’s a postcard again. HTTPS is the locked box: it stays shut the whole way.This lesson: Watch›Learn›PracticeQuick factsDoesseals your traffic in a tunnel to a VPN serverProtectsyour device to the VPN server, not beyondThe network you’re on seesfor traffic in the tunnel, only that you’re talking to the VPN serverKinds includeremote access (device to network) and site-to-site (network to network)One way to build itIPsec, with IKE and ESP

Watch · Step 2 of 5IKE: Setting Up the TunnelYour laptop and the VPN server agree on keysNow you turn the VPN on. Your laptop and the VPN server, at 203.0.113.40, first agree on secret keys, in a way someone listening can’t work out. Then each proves who it is, already encrypted, and the server gives your laptop an address on its side: 203.0.113.41. This is IKE, the part of IPsec that sets up the tunnel.Go deeperthe technical detailsHere a NAT is in the way: it swaps your laptop’s address and port for its own. Watch · Step 3 of 5ESP: Wrapped and SealedOne packet inside anotherYou open example.net again. This time your laptop wraps the request: the whole packet, from 203.0.113.41 to example.net, is encrypted and put inside a new packet addressed to the VPN server. That’s ESP. Someone listening on the café’s Wi-Fi sees only the outside: a packet from you to 203.0.113.40. Where it’s really going, and what it says, stay sealed.Go deeperthe technical detailsThis is IPsec’s tunnel mode. ESP encrypts the whole original packet, its header too, and the new header names only the tunnel’s two ends.
